AI.conclusion: The cycle-consistent neural surrogate enables fast, accurate, and invertible edge plasma modeling suitable for real-time control, parameter scans, uncertainty analysis, and digital twins of tokamak exhaust systems.

title: Free-volume origin of diverging direct correlations in hard crystals: insights from an exact one-dimensional model
summary: Second order direct correlation functions in three-dimensional hard-sphere crystals have much larger amplitudes (of the order of $1/n_{\mathrm{vac}}$ where $n_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the vacancy concentration) and a more strongly structured spatial form of apparent shorter range than their liquid-state counterparts. We separate the two underlying questions---why the correlations are large and why they have the form they do---using the exact one-dimensional Percus functional for hard rods. A periodic crystal-like density is represented by Gaussian peaks with occupation probability $q=1-n_{\mathrm{vac}}$. The relevant thermodynamic quantity is the local insertion free volume $A(x)$. Its minimum can be written as $A_{\mathrm{min}} =Δ_{αa}+(1-Δ_{αa})n_{\mathrm{vac}}$, where $Δ_{αa}$ is the residual free volume at full occupation caused by finite localization (characterized by a width parameter $α$) and lattice spacing $a$. The first and second direct correlations therefore contain the singular dependences $c^{(1)}\sim\ln A_{\mathrm{min}} $ and $c^{(2)} \sim-1/A_{\mathrm{min}} $. The observed $1/n_{\mathrm{vac}}$ dependence is the vacancy-dominated limit $n_{\mathrm{vac}}\ggΔ_{αa}$, rather than the most general result. The spatial form of $c^{(2)}$ has a separate geometrical origin: the hard-rod weight functions select configurations in which exclusion intervals and their boundaries intersect regions of small free volume. This produces plateaus, edges, and localized ridges tied to the underlying periodic density. A numerical solution of the inhomogeneous Ornstein--Zernike equation shows how these singular direct correlations are redistributed in the total and pair correlations. The model provides a minimal free-volume explanation for both the magnitude and the lattice-specific form of crystalline direct correlation functions.

AI.tldr: This paper explains why direct correlation functions in 3D hard-sphere crystals have large amplitudes (~1/n_vac) and characteristic spatial forms, using a 1D Percus functional model with Gaussian peaks. The key insight separates magnitude (from local free volume minima) from spatial structure (from geometrical selection by hard-rod weight functions).
AI.motivation: To understand why second-order direct correlation functions in hard-sphere crystals exhibit anomalously large amplitudes (scaling as 1/n_vac) and strongly structured, apparently short-range spatial forms, which differ markedly from liquid-state correlations.
AI.method: Uses the exact one-dimensional Percus functional for hard rods with periodic Gaussian density peaks (occupation probability q=1-n_vac). Derives local insertion free volume A(x) and its minimum A_min = Δ_αa + (1-Δ_αa)n_vac. Shows singular dependences c^(1) ~ ln A_min and c^(2) ~ -1/A_min. Analyzes spatial structure via hard-rod weight functions selecting configurations where exclusion intervals intersect small free-volume regions, producing plateaus, edges, and ridges. Solves inhomogeneous Ornstein-Zernike equation numerically.
AI.result: The 1/n_vac scaling is the vacancy-dominated limit (n_vac >> Δ_αa), not the most general result. The spatial form of c^(2) has a separate geometrical origin from hard-rod weight functions. The model redistributes singular direct correlations into total and pair correlations via the Ornstein-Zernike equation.
AI.conclusion: A minimal free-volume explanation successfully captures both the magnitude and lattice-specific form of crystalline direct correlation functions, separating the thermodynamic (free volume) and geometric (weight function) origins.

title: A high-dimensional neural network potential for finite-temperature phenomena in NiTi martensite
summary: We present a high-dimensional neural network potential (HDNNP) for the martensitic phase of the NiTi shape-memory alloy trained to density functional theory (DFT) data. A central aspect of this work is the systematic validation of the potential with respect to the underlying DFT reference method for key properties governing structural evolution, including equilibrium crystal structures, elastic constants, generalized-stacking fault energies, and vibrational spectra. The HDNNP accurately describes the relative stability of the B19$^\prime$ and B33 phases, including subtle energy differences on the order of meV/atom. The predicted stacking-fault energy landscape is strongly anisotropic and reveals a preferential shear pathway, providing atomistic insight into deformation and twinning mechanisms. Finite-temperature molecular dynamics simulations further enable the investigation of unconstrained structural evolution as a function of temperature. Overall, the developed HDNNP provides a robust basis for atomistic simulations of the complex structural and functional behavior of martensitic NiTi systems containing hundreds of thousands of atoms on nanosecond time scales.

AI.tldr: A high-dimensional neural network potential (HDNNP) for martensitic NiTi shape-memory alloy is developed and systematically validated against DFT, accurately capturing phase stability, anisotropic stacking-fault energies, and enabling large-scale finite-temperature MD simulations.
AI.motivation: To enable large-scale atomistic simulations of the complex structural and functional behavior of martensitic NiTi shape-memory alloys, which require accurate interatomic potentials that capture subtle energy differences and deformation mechanisms beyond the reach of DFT.
AI.method: A high-dimensional neural network potential (HDNNP) trained to DFT data, systematically validated for equilibrium structures, elastic constants, generalized-stacking fault energies, and vibrational spectra; combined with finite-temperature molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.result: The HDNNP accurately describes the relative stability of B19' and B33 phases with meV/atom precision, reveals a strongly anisotropic stacking-fault energy landscape with a preferential shear pathway, and enables nanosecond-scale simulations of hundreds of thousands of atoms.
AI.conclusion: The developed HDNNP is a robust tool for atomistic simulations of martensitic NiTi systems, providing insight into deformation, twinning mechanisms, and temperature-dependent structural evolution at large scales.

title: Plasma screening and configuration interaction effects induced large enhancement on L-shell photoionization cross sections and opacity
comment: Main text: 6 pages, 5 figures; Supplemental Material: 3 pages, 2 figures
summary: An opacity model that incorporates improved treatments of both plasma screening and configuration interaction (CI) effects is proposed, and a 25-30% enhancement on the iron L-shell opacity is predicted at solar interior temperatures. It is originated from the plasma screening induced 14-17% enhancement on the photoionization cross sections and the CI induced 10-20% enhancement on photoexcitation and photoionization cross sections for open L-shell ions. These explain the long-standing discrepancy between theoretical and experimental iron opacity [Nature 517, 56], and the relatively weaker enhancements on chromium and nickel opacity [Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 235001] due to the sensitivity of these effects to the different L-shell electron population and plasma temperature/density. This letter provides the systematic interpretation of L-shell opacity measurements at solar interior temperatures, and advances the accurate simulation of opacity and radiative transport in high-energy-density plasma.

AI.tldr: A new opacity model combining improved plasma screening and configuration interaction (CI) effects predicts a 25-30% enhancement in iron L-shell opacity at solar interior temperatures, resolving the long-standing discrepancy between theoretical and experimental iron opacity measurements.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing discrepancy between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements of iron opacity at solar interior temperatures, and to systematically interpret L-shell opacity measurements for iron, chromium, and nickel.
AI.method: An opacity model incorporating improved treatments of both plasma screening effects (yielding 14-17% enhancement on photoionization cross sections) and configuration interaction effects (yielding 10-20% enhancement on photoexcitation and photoionization cross sections for open L-shell ions).
AI.result: A 25-30% enhancement on iron L-shell opacity at solar interior temperatures, with weaker enhancements on chromium and nickel opacity due to sensitivity of these effects to L-shell electron population and plasma conditions.
AI.conclusion: The model provides a systematic interpretation of L-shell opacity measurements at solar interior temperatures and advances the accurate simulation of opacity and radiative transport in high-energy-density plasma.

title: Exact Nagaoka-to-spiral transition in the doped infinite-U triangular lattice
summary: We study the single-hole infinite-$U$ Hubbard model on the triangular lattice with nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor hoppings $t_1$ and $t_2$. A frustrating $t_2$ destabilizes Nagaoka ferromagnetism through a Lifshitz transition to a long-wavelength coplanar spiral at $t_{2,c}/t_1=-0.182$. We determine the critical point analytically by reducing the many-body problem to an effective two-body hole--magnon scattering problem in which the hard-core hole--magnon constraint is treated exactly. Numerical calculations confirm the spiral ground state and reveal a coherent spin polaron with quasiparticle weight $Z\simeq0.92$ at the Lifshitz-shifted momentum $\mathbf{K}=-\mathbf{Q}^*$. These results establish the first quantum instability of the triangular-lattice Nagaoka ferromagnet and provide the magnetic baseline for magnon-mediated pairing at finite doping.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that frustrating next-nearest-neighbor hopping destabilizes Nagaoka ferromagnetism on the triangular lattice via a Lifshitz transition to a coplanar spiral at $t_{2,c}/t_1=-0.182$, determined analytically through hole-magnon scattering, with numerical confirmation of a coherent spin polaron ($Z\simeq0.92$).
AI.motivation: To identify the first quantum instability of the triangular-lattice Nagaoka ferromagnet and establish the magnetic baseline for magnon-mediated pairing at finite doping.
AI.method: Analytical reduction of the many-body problem to an effective two-body hole-magnon scattering problem with exact hard-core constraint, combined with numerical calculations to confirm the spiral ground state.
AI.result: The critical point for the Lifshitz transition is $t_{2,c}/t_1=-0.182$; the spiral ground state is confirmed numerically; the quasiparticle weight at the shifted momentum is $Z\simeq0.92$.
AI.conclusion: Frustrating $t_2$ destabilizes Nagaoka ferromagnetism via a Lifshitz transition to a long-wavelength coplanar spiral, providing a baseline for magnon-mediated pairing at finite doping.

title: Machine Learning for Charge State Characterization of Isolated Double Quantum Dots
summary: Scaling semiconductor quantum dot arrays toward fault-tolerant quantum computing requires efficient tuneup of spin qubits, a process that depends on the analysis of charge stability maps (CSMs) and remains largely manual. While machine learning has been widely applied to CSM analysis in reservoir-coupled devices, automated tuning in the increasingly important isolated-mode regime has received limited attention. In isolated-mode CSMs, charge transitions appear as near-vertical lines, making them well suited to compact, task-specific models. We present two convolutional neural networks with fewer than one million parameters, trained on CSMs collected from 32 silicon metal-oxide-semiconductor (SiMOS) double-quantum-dot devices measured at approximately 1 K using an automated cryogenic probing system. Sixteen devices were used for training and sixteen were held out to evaluate cross-device generalization against hand-labeled ground truth. CSMClassifier identifies charge instability and sensor artifacts, achieving 94% macro-averaged accuracy across three quality classes on 2,407 held-out images. ChargeLineNet localizes charge-transition lines and determines electron occupancy, achieving 95.3% exact line-count accuracy on 1,131 held-out images. Combined into a single pipeline, the models correctly determine electron occupancy for 93.8% of clean held-out images. Pre-training on synthetic images substantially improves label efficiency. Fine-tuning the pre-trained model on limited experimental data maintains over 90% accuracy, whereas training from scratch degrades significantly under the same conditions. Together, the two models occupy only 6.5 MB and process images in less than 60 ms on standard laboratory hardware, demonstrating a practical path toward scalable, automated characterization and tuneup of quantum-dot devices.

AI.tldr: Two compact convolutional neural networks (CSMClassifier and ChargeLineNet, <1M parameters each, 6.5 MB total) automate analysis of charge stability maps in isolated-mode silicon quantum-dot arrays, achieving 94% quality classification accuracy and 95.3% exact line-count accuracy, with robust cross-device generalization across 32 devices and practical real-time performance (<60 ms per image).
AI.motivation: Scaling semiconductor quantum dot arrays for fault-tolerant quantum computing requires automated tuneup of spin qubits, but isolated-mode charge stability map analysis—critical for modern isolated-mode devices—remains largely manual and underexplored by machine learning methods.
AI.method: Two CNNs (<1M parameters each) trained on experimental CSMs from 32 SiMOS double-quantum-dot devices (16 train, 16 test) via automated cryogenic probing at ~1 K. CSMClassifier detects charge instability and sensor artifacts (3-class quality classification). ChargeLineNet localizes charge-transition lines and determines electron occupancy. Includes synthetic pre-training for label efficiency.
AI.result: CSMClassifier: 94% macro-averaged accuracy on 2,407 held-out images. ChargeLineNet: 95.3% exact line-count accuracy on 1,131 held-out images. Combined pipeline: 93.8% correct electron occupancy on clean images. Pre-training on synthetic data maintains >90% accuracy with limited experimental data; from-scratch training degrades significantly. Inference <60 ms, model size 6.5 MB.
AI.conclusion: The proposed lightweight two-model pipeline offers a practical, scalable path toward automated characterization and tuneup of quantum-dot devices, addressing a key bottleneck in fault-tolerant quantum computing hardware scaling.

title: Doping-induced Ferromagnetic order and its unusual evolution to Helical Antiferromagnetic Order in Sr(Ni$_{1-x}$Co$_x$)$_2$P$_2$
summary: SrNi$_2$P$_2$ represents a unique case of a collapsed structural phase (one-third collapsed, where one out of every three P-P pairs forms a bond) in the A(TM)$_2$X$_2$ family of compounds (A = alkali metal, alkaline-earth metal, or rare earth; TM = transition metal; X = pnictogen). Furthermore, Co doping studies aimed at understanding the interrelationship between this unusual bonding motif and the resulting physical properties produced a magnetically rich phase diagram, specifically on the Co-rich side of the phase diagram. However, important questions remained regarding the detailed nature of the magnetic ground states. To address these issues, we performed single-crystal neutron diffraction measurements on Sr(Ni$_{1-x}$Co$_x$)$_2$P$_2$ with compositions $x = 0.88$, 0.94, and 0.97. For $x = 0.88$ and 0.94, the measurements reveal incommensurate helical magnetic order with a doping-dependent propagation vector $(0,0,τ)$, similar to that observed in Sr(Ni$_{1-x}$Co$_x$)$_2$As$_2$. In contrast, the $x = 0.97$ composition shows clear signatures of a ferromagnetically ordered ground state, resolving the earlier ambiguity regarding the nature of the low-temperature phase. Furthermore, our results highlight the subtle balance between these competing ground states, whose evolution does not appear to be fully captured by the conventional frameworks of either itinerant or local-moment Heisenberg models typically applied to related 122 systems.

AI.tldr: Neutron diffraction on Sr(Ni$_{1-x}$Co$_x$)$_2$P$_2$ reveals incommensurate helical order for $x=0.88,0.94$ and ferromagnetic order for $x=0.97$, resolving magnetic ground state ambiguities in the Co-rich phase diagram.
AI.motivation: To resolve questions about the detailed nature of magnetic ground states in Co-doped SrNi$_2$P$_2$, particularly on the Co-rich side of the phase diagram, where prior studies had left ambiguity.
AI.method: Single-crystal neutron diffraction measurements on Sr(Ni$_{1-x}$Co$_x$)$_2$P$_2$ at three compositions ($x=0.88$, 0.94, 0.97).
AI.result: For $x=0.88$ and 0.94, incommensurate helical magnetic order with doping-dependent $(0,0,τ)$ propagation vector; for $x=0.97$, ferromagnetic order. The evolution of competing ground states is not fully captured by conventional itinerant or local-moment Heisenberg frameworks.
AI.conclusion: The magnetic ground states in this system are subtly balanced, and their evolution challenges standard models (itinerant or local-moment Heisenberg) typically applied to 122-type compounds.

title: Determination of fundamental properties of nitrogen from first principles. III. Temperature and frequency dependence of the molecular polarizability and magnetic susceptibility
summary: This work is the third part of the series of papers that focus on the theoretical determination of the properties of nitrogen that are relevant in metrology. Here we present first-principles calculations of the temperature and frequency dependence of the molecular polarizability and magnetic susceptibility of the nitrogen molecule (N$_2$). The purely electronic contributions to the static polarizability, Cauchy coefficients (up to sixth order), and isotropic magnetic susceptibility are computed over a range of internuclear distances using a robust composite scheme combining several electronic structure methods. The temperature dependence, evaluated from $50$~K to $2000$~K, is determined using two independent methods: rovibrational averaging and path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC). The polarizabilities obtained from theory agree with the recent high-precision thermometry measurements, wherever the latter are available, but are significantly less accurate. However, the main usefulness of the theoretical data revolves around combining it with the available experimental results to generate semi-empirical estimates of various quantities that have never been measured thus far. As an example, we determine highly accurate semi-empirical estimates of the static polarizability at key reference temperatures, $α_0(T)=11.735\,962$~a.u.\ at $T=303$~K and $α_0(T)=11.735\,585$~a.u.\ at $T=273.16$~K. Furthermore, we report theoretical values for the magnetic susceptibility, highlighting the importance of the paramagnetic contribution, and address a significant discrepancy with the experimental data for this quantity.

AI.tldr: This third-part paper presents first-principles calculations of the temperature and frequency dependence of the molecular polarizability and magnetic susceptibility of N₂, using a composite electronic structure scheme and two independent methods (rovibrational averaging and PIMC) for temperature dependence from 50–2000 K. While theoretical polarizabilities agree with experiments but are less accurate, the data is useful for generating semi-empirical estimates of unmeasured quantities (e.g., static polarizability at key temperatures). The study also reports theoretical magnetic susceptibility values, highlighting the paramagnetic contribution and addressing a discrepancy with experimental data.
AI.motivation: To theoretically determine the properties of nitrogen relevant to metrology, specifically the temperature- and frequency-dependent molecular polarizability and magnetic susceptibility of N₂, and to resolve discrepancies with experimental data while providing semi-empirical estimates for quantities not yet measured.
AI.method: Composite electronic structure scheme combining several methods for purely electronic contributions to static polarizability, Cauchy coefficients (up to sixth order), and isotropic magnetic susceptibility over a range of internuclear distances. Temperature dependence (50–2000 K) evaluated via two independent methods: rovibrational averaging and path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC).
AI.result: Theoretical polarizabilities agree with high-precision thermometry measurements but are significantly less accurate. Highly accurate semi-empirical estimates of static polarizability at reference temperatures were obtained: α₀(303 K)=11.735962 a.u. and α₀(273.16 K)=11.735585 a.u. Theoretical magnetic susceptibility values highlight the importance of the paramagnetic contribution and address a significant discrepancy with experimental data.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical data is most useful when combined with experimental results to generate semi-empirical estimates of unmeasured quantities. The paramagnetic contribution to magnetic susceptibility is critical, and the study resolves a notable discrepancy with experimental data for this quantity.

title: Optimal feedback control under stepwise equilibration and partial observation
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary Information: 13 pages, 1 figure
summary: Many microscopic machines rely on noisy signals to direct nonequilibrium transformations and operate in a timescale-separated regime. We consider feedback protocols in which a system equilibrates between rapid, measurement-conditioned changes of its energy landscape. In this limit, the partially observable control problem reduces exactly to a finite-horizon Bellman recursion over Hamiltonian updates. For a harmonic trap translated to a prescribed target under noisy position measurements, we solve this recursion analytically. The optimal protocol balances its response to the estimated fluctuation against progress toward the target, exploiting information early while enforcing the endpoint near the deadline. The minimum work decomposes into a positive thermodynamic-length transport cost and a negative information-enabled extraction term set by the fraction of equilibrium fluctuations resolved by the measurement. When a fixed intervention cost exceeds the asymptotic extraction per cycle, it selects a finite optimal number of cycles. We show that, in this translated harmonic case, the minimum thermodynamic cost of creating and resetting the measurement record always exceeds this threshold, making the optimal cycle count finite and the net work non-negative for any measurement channel.

AI.tldr: This paper analytically solves optimal feedback control for a harmonic trap under noisy measurements, showing the optimal protocol balances fluctuation response against target progress, and demonstrates that measurement costs make the optimal number of cycles finite and net work non-negative.
AI.motivation: Microscopic machines often rely on noisy signals for nonequilibrium transformations in a timescale-separated regime. The paper aims to understand optimal feedback protocols that minimize work when controlling a system under partial observability with noisy measurements.
AI.method: The authors consider feedback protocols where the system equilibrates between rapid measurement-conditioned energy landscape changes. They show the partially observable control problem reduces to a finite-horizon Bellman recursion over Hamiltonian updates. For a harmonic trap translated to a target under noisy position measurements, they solve this recursion analytically.
AI.result: The optimal protocol balances response to estimated fluctuation against progress toward the target. Minimum work decomposes into a positive thermodynamic-length transport cost and a negative information-enabled extraction term. A fixed intervention cost selects a finite optimal number of cycles when it exceeds the asymptotic extraction per cycle. For the translated harmonic trap, the minimum cost of creating/resetting the measurement record always exceeds this threshold, making the optimal cycle count finite and net work non-negative.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides an analytically solvable model of optimal feedback control in microscopic systems, revealing fundamental trade-offs between information, work extraction, and intervention costs. The results imply that measurement costs impose a fundamental bound ensuring non-negative net work in such systems.

title: Analytical Forces from the Bethe-Salpeter Equation for Large-Scale Excited-State Relaxation
summary: We present an efficient plane-wave implementation of analytical nuclear forces for electronic excited states described by the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE). The formulation combines density-matrix perturbation theory with a Lagrangian approach, and avoids both explicit empty-state summations and the response calculations for each atomic displacement, required by conventional approaches based on density functional perturbation theory. Together with GPU acceleration, these advances make BSE forces calculations tractable for solid-state systems containing hundreds of atoms. We demonstrate the method on two point defects with distinct dielectric environments: the nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond, where BSE and time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) yield consistent excited-state relaxations, and the carbon-dimer defect in two-dimensional hexagonal boron nitride, where the screened electron-hole interaction included in the BSE stabilizes the localized defect excitation and corrects the relaxation pattern predicted by semilocal TDDFT. These results establish a scalable framework for BSE-level studies of excited-state relaxation and vibronic coupling in heterogeneous condensed systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an efficient plane-wave implementation of analytical nuclear forces for BSE excited states, using density-matrix perturbation theory and a Lagrangian approach to avoid empty-state summations and per-displacement response calculations. GPU acceleration makes it tractable for hundreds of atoms. Demonstrated on NV center in diamond and carbon-dimer defect in 2D hBN, showing BSE corrects relaxation patterns predicted by semilocal TDDFT.
AI.motivation: To develop a scalable computational method for calculating excited-state forces at the BSE level, enabling studies of excited-state relaxation and vibronic coupling in heterogeneous condensed systems with hundreds of atoms, which was previously intractable due to high computational cost.
AI.method: Combines density-matrix perturbation theory with a Lagrangian approach, avoids explicit empty-state summations and per-atomic-displacement response calculations, and leverages GPU acceleration. Implemented in a plane-wave basis.
AI.result: For the NV center in diamond, BSE and TDDFT yield consistent excited-state relaxations. For the carbon-dimer defect in 2D hBN, the screened electron-hole interaction in BSE stabilizes the localized defect excitation and corrects the relaxation pattern predicted by semilocal TDDFT.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a scalable framework for BSE-level studies of excited-state relaxation and vibronic coupling in heterogeneous condensed systems.

title: Experimental realization of a rotating radio-frequency ion trap for precision metrology
summary: We discuss the experimental realization of the rotating radio-frequency (rrf) trap, proposed by Hasegawa and Bollinger [Phys. Rev. A 72, 043403 (2005)]. Compared to a traditional linear rf (lrf) Paul trap, the rrf trap is a closer analogy to the popular mechanical lecture demonstration for a Paul trap. In an ion trap with reslistic, non-ideal electrode geometry, the rrf trap averages over angular variations in the effective potential. This averaging provides more uniform confinement and reduces ion loss at equal confinement strength compared with the lrf trap. This feature makes the rrf trap configuration advantageous for precision metrology application, such as electron electric dipole moment (eEDM) measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally realizes the rotating radio-frequency (rrf) ion trap, which offers more uniform confinement and reduced ion loss compared to traditional linear rf traps, making it advantageous for precision metrology like eEDM measurements.
AI.motivation: To experimentally realize the rotating radio-frequency (rrf) trap proposed earlier and demonstrate its advantages over the traditional linear rf Paul trap, particularly for precision metrology applications such as electron electric dipole moment (eEDM) measurements.
AI.method: Experimental realization of the rrf trap design proposed by Hasegawa and Bollinger, with comparison to a traditional linear rf (lrf) Paul trap under realistic, non-ideal electrode geometry conditions.
AI.result: The rrf trap averages over angular variations in the effective potential, providing more uniform confinement and reducing ion loss at equal confinement strength compared to the lrf trap.
AI.conclusion: The rrf trap configuration is advantageous for precision metrology applications such as eEDM measurements due to its superior confinement uniformity and reduced ion loss.

title: End-State-Controlled Quantum Transport in Armchair Graphene Nanoribbon Artificial Quantum Materials
summary: Artificial quantum materials based on atomically precise graphene nanostructures provide an ideal platform for exploring quantum phenomena arising from localized electronic states. Here, we develop a real-space theoretical framework to elucidate the microscopic origin of interface states in graphene architectures composed of $n$-triangulenes and armchair graphene nanoribbons (AGNRs). By continuously tuning the coupling between graphene building blocks, we reveal the evolution of triangulene zero-energy modes and AGNR end states into compact localized node orbitals at three-arm junctions. The number and chirality of these node orbitals obey a universal relation, $N_{node,δ}=|N_{es,t,A(B)}-N_{tri,0,B(A)}|$, where $N_{es,t}$ denotes the total number of AGNR end states contributed by the three AGNR arms at the junction, and $N_{tri,0}$ is the number of zero-energy modes of the attached triangulene. The chirality of the node orbitals is determined by the dominant constituent: when $N_{es,t}>N_{tri,0}$, they inherit the sublattice chirality of the AGNR end states ($δ=A(B)$), whereas for $N_{tri,0}>N_{es,t}$ they inherit that of the triangulene zero-energy modes ($δ=B(A)$). This real-space picture provides a transparent understanding of compact localized state (CLS) formation beyond conventional bulk topological descriptions. Using experimentally synthesized triangulene nanographenes as representative examples, we further explain the emergence of their zero-energy modes and quantitatively reproduce their tunneling spectra within an extended Anderson model. Finally, we demonstrate that these node orbitals can serve as elementary building blocks for constructing artificial graphene nanoribbons with highly tunable flat subbands near the Fermi energy. The resulting CLSs exhibit controllable degeneracy and strongly anisotropic quantum transport.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a real-space theoretical framework to explain interface states in graphene nanostructures composed of triangulenes and armchair graphene nanoribbons, revealing a universal relation for compact localized node orbitals and demonstrating their use as building blocks for artificial graphene nanoribbons with tunable flat subbands and anisotropic transport.
AI.motivation: To elucidate the microscopic origin of interface states in graphene architectures built from triangulenes and AGNRs, and to provide a real-space understanding of compact localized state formation beyond conventional bulk topological descriptions.
AI.method: A real-space theoretical framework is developed to tune coupling between graphene building blocks, deriving a universal relation $N_{node,δ}=|N_{es,t,A(B)}-N_{tri,0,B(A)}|$ that governs the number and chirality of compact localized node orbitals at three-arm junctions. An extended Anderson model is used to reproduce tunneling spectra.
AI.result: The evolution of triangulene zero-energy modes and AGNR end states into compact localized node orbitals is revealed. The node orbitals obey a universal relation with chirality determined by the dominant constituent. The framework quantitatively reproduces experimental tunneling spectra and demonstrates that these node orbitals can construct artificial graphene nanoribbons with tunable flat subbands and strongly anisotropic transport.
AI.conclusion: The real-space picture provides a transparent understanding of CLS formation, and the node orbitals serve as elementary building blocks for designing artificial graphene nanoribbons with controllable degeneracy and anisotropic quantum transport properties.

title: Graph Neural Network Force Fields (GPTFF-mol) for Organic Molecules from Optimization Trajectories (OpenGEM26)
summary: Density functional theory (DFT) serves as a reliable tool for atomistic molecular simulations, while machine learning potentials have become powerful complements to balance accuracy and efficiency. In this work, we release OpenGEM26 (Open Generated Ensemble of Molecules, 2026), a large-scale dataset comprising 200,000 unique molecules and 4.4 million conformations composed of H, C, N, O, S and Cl with up to ten heavy atoms. All calculations are carried out at the ωB97X-D/Def2-SVP and Def2-TZVP levels with dispersion corrections, and complete structural optimization trajectories and abundant non-equilibrium structures are recorded. Statistical analyses confirm that this dataset covers a broader conformational space than QM9 in terms of energy, bond lengths and bond angles. A graph neural network-based potential GPTFF-mol is trained using the new dataset, achieving an energy mean absolute error of 16 meV/molecule, which is equivalent to 0.82meV/atom, and superior force prediction performance compared with ANI-2x. Validated by butane rotation and keto-enol tautomerization tests, the model accurately describes molecular dynamical behaviors and reaction barriers at distorted geometries. This work provides a high-quality resource and robust ML potential for efficient simulations of sulfur- and chlorine-containing organic molecules.

AI.tldr: OpenGEM26 is a large-scale dataset of 200K molecules and 4.4M conformations (H, C, N, O, S, Cl) computed at ωB97X-D/Def2-SVP and Def2-TZVP levels, with a GNN-based potential GPTFF-mol achieving 0.82 meV/atom energy MAE and superior force accuracy over ANI-2x for sulfur/chlorine organic simulations.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of high-quality, conformationally diverse datasets and machine learning potentials for organic molecules containing sulfur and chlorine, which are underrepresented in existing resources like QM9.
AI.method: Generated 200,000 unique molecules and 4.4M conformations (up to 10 heavy atoms: H, C, N, O, S, Cl) using DFT at ωB97X-D/Def2-SVP and Def2-TZVP levels with dispersion corrections, recording full optimization trajectories and non-equilibrium structures. A graph neural network-based potential, GPTFF-mol, was trained on this dataset.
AI.result: Dataset covers broader conformational space than QM9 in energy, bond lengths, and bond angles. GPTFF-mol achieves 16 meV/molecule (0.82 meV/atom) energy MAE and superior force prediction over ANI-2x. Validated on butane rotation and keto-enol tautomerization tests.
AI.conclusion: OpenGEM26 provides a high-quality resource for sulfur- and chlorine-containing organic molecules, and GPTFF-mol serves as a robust ML potential for efficient and accurate molecular simulations.

title: Gaplessness indicator by topologically trivial twisting operators
summary: We propose several general necessary conditions for quantum many-body system in one dimension respecting U(1) symmetry to be gapped. We show that the ground-state expectation value of topologically trivial twisting operators must approach unity in the thermodynamic limit with a certain finite-size scaling. Equivalently, its violation can indicate gaplessness of U(1)-symmetric Hamiltonians. The topological triviality of such a twisting operator enables us to derive infinitely many other gaplessness indicators by static structure factor to any order in real experiments, which are impossible to obtain by earlier topologically nontrivial twisting operators. We also apply analytic and numerical calculations to test the efficiency and consistency of our results.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes necessary conditions for 1D U(1)-symmetric quantum many-body systems to be gapped, showing that topologically trivial twisting operators' expectation values must approach unity in the thermodynamic limit, and derives infinitely many gaplessness indicators from the static structure factor.
AI.motivation: To establish general necessary conditions for gapped phases in 1D U(1)-symmetric quantum many-body systems and to derive experimentally accessible gaplessness indicators beyond earlier topologically nontrivial approaches.
AI.method: Derivation of necessary conditions based on topologically trivial twisting operators' ground-state expectation values and their finite-size scaling in the thermodynamic limit; construction of infinitely many gaplessness indicators from the static structure factor; analytic and numerical validation.
AI.result: The ground-state expectation value of topologically trivial twisting operators must approach unity in the thermodynamic limit with specific finite-size scaling for gapped systems; violation indicates gaplessness; infinitely many gaplessness indicators derived from the static structure factor.
AI.conclusion: Topologically trivial twisting operators provide a powerful framework for detecting gaplessness in U(1)-symmetric 1D systems, overcoming limitations of previous topologically nontrivial operators, and enabling practical experimental detection via static structure factor measurements.

title: First-principles calculation of electron-phonon spectral functions for defects using phonon interpolation
summary: Point defects in wide-band-gap semiconductors exhibit optical spectra strongly shaped by electron-phonon coupling, but direct first-principles calculation of the corresponding phonon sidebands is often limited by the coarse vibrational spectrum of the largest defect supercells accessible by ab-initio electronic structure codes. In this work, we present a phonon-interpolation method for Huang-Rhys spectral densities and optical lineshape functions on hypercells created by extending the defect-containing supercells on arbitrarily dense phonon $q$-point grids. The method is based on reconstructing the transition-induced force associated with the optical excitation and using this localized force source to couple the defect transition to a densely sampled vibrational continuum. In this formulation, the local defect physics is obtained from ab initio supercell calculations, while the long-wavelength acoustic modes and the detailed structure of the host phonon spectrum are recovered by diagonalizing interpolated dynamical matrices in large hypercells. We demonstrate the method on the negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy centre in diamond between its ground $^{3}A_{2}$ and excited $^{3}E$ states. The transition-force is shown to be strongly localized around the defect, with converged localization measures obtained in a $4\times4\times4$ supercell accessible by density functional theory calculations. We interpolate the electron-phonon coupling on hypercells up to $32\times32\times32$ corresponding to approximately 17 million atoms, thereby recovering smooth, continuous Huang-Rhys spectral densities with ultrafine spectral resolution. The dominant coupling band is found near 63~meV; the low-energy acoustic contribution follows the expected linear scaling; and we recover the finer van-Hove-related structures in the optical phonon regime observed in experiments.

AI.tldr: A phonon-interpolation method is developed to compute Huang-Rhys spectral densities and optical lineshapes on hypercells with arbitrarily dense phonon q-point grids, enabling first-principles calculation of phonon sidebands in wide-band-gap semiconductors beyond the limitations of coarse defect supercells. Demonstrated on the NV⁻ center in diamond, it recovers smooth spectral densities with ultrafine resolution using hypercells up to ~17 million atoms.
AI.motivation: Point defects in wide-band-gap semiconductors exhibit optical spectra strongly shaped by electron-phonon coupling, but direct first-principles calculation of phonon sidebands is limited by the coarse vibrational spectrum of the largest defect supercells accessible by ab-initio methods.
AI.method: The method reconstructs the transition-induced force associated with optical excitation, using this localized force source to couple the defect transition to a densely sampled vibrational continuum. Local defect physics is obtained from ab-initio supercell calculations, while long-wavelength acoustic modes and detailed host phonon structure are recovered by diagonalizing interpolated dynamical matrices in large hypercells.
AI.result: Demonstrated on the NV⁻ center in diamond (³A₂ → ³E transition). Transition-force is strongly localized, converged in a 4×4×4 supercell. Interpolation on hypercells up to 32×32×32 (~17 million atoms) yields smooth, continuous Huang-Rhys spectral densities with ultrafine resolution. Dominant coupling band at ~63 meV; low-energy acoustic contribution follows linear scaling; finer van-Hove-related structures in the optical phonon regime are recovered.
AI.conclusion: The phonon-interpolation method overcomes the vibrational coarseness limitation of defect supercells, enabling accurate first-principles phonon sideband calculations with fine spectral resolution, validated against experimental observations.

title: Long-wavelength density response and momentum resolution in strange-metal charge spectroscopy
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, 1 table; accepted for publication in Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter
summary: Momentum-resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) on strange-metal Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+x}$ (Bi-2212) observes a broad charge continuum that is nearly momentum independent over an extended finite-momentum regime, whereas optical spectroscopy determines a metallic local conductivity. We analyze the long-wavelength response function that connects these regimes: the proper homogeneous bulk charge-density polarization. For any homogeneous $U(1)$-conserving metal whose longitudinal matter conductivity remains finite in the $q\to0$ limit at fixed nonzero frequency, the Ward identity gives $χ''_{ρρ}({\bf q},ω)=q^2\operatorname{Re}σ_L({\bf q},ω)/ω$. We then prove that any nonnegative normalized momentum-resolution kernel with a self-similar $q$-scaled profile, uniformly bounded second moment, and tight second-moment tails preserves this $q^2$ asymptotic behavior, changing only the prefactor. Consequently, a nearly local finite-$q$ continuum in Bi-2212, if continuously connected to a regular metallic optical limit of the same proper bulk response, is naturally described by a crossover surface $q_\ast(ω,T)$. The theorem is a constraint on the proper bulk density response, or on a positive $q$-scaled convolution of it; screened loss functions and surface EELS observables require the corresponding electrodynamic conversion before the constraint is applied.

AI.tldr: This paper proves a theorem linking momentum-resolved EELS charge continua in strange metals to the optical metallic limit via Ward identity and self-similar kernel constraints, establishing that a nearly local finite-q continuum arises from a crossover surface q*(ω,T) when continuously connected to a regular metallic bulk response.
AI.motivation: To reconcile the seemingly contradictory observations of a broad, nearly momentum-independent charge continuum at finite momentum in Bi-2212 (from momentum-resolved EELS) with the metallic local conductivity seen in optical spectroscopy, by analyzing the proper homogeneous bulk charge-density polarization that connects these regimes.
AI.method: Uses the Ward identity to show that for any homogeneous U(1)-conserving metal, the density response χ''ρρ(q,ω) = q² Re σ_L(q,ω)/ω in the q→0 limit. Then proves a theorem: any nonnegative, normalized momentum-resolution kernel with a self-similar q-scaled profile, uniformly bounded second moment, and tight tails preserves this q² asymptotic behavior, modifying only the prefactor.
AI.result: A nearly local finite-q charge continuum in Bi-2212, if continuously connected to a regular metallic optical limit of the same proper bulk response, is naturally described by a crossover surface q*(ω,T). The theorem acts as a constraint on the proper bulk density response or on a positive q-scaled convolution of it.
AI.conclusion: The observed momentum-independent broad continuum in Bi-2212 does not contradict the optical metallic behavior when viewed through the lens of the proper bulk response; however, screened loss functions and surface EELS observables require electrodynamic conversion before applying the constraint.

title: Exceptional-Point Geometry of Weak Topological Boundary States
summary: In this article, we demonstrate that weak topology can be formulated geometrically in terms of exceptional singularities of an analytically continued Bloch Hamiltonian. A general plaquette chiral model in two dimensions serves as a minimal realization of dual weak topology, possessing two independent families of weak topological invariants, one for each spatial direction. The weak-topological edge states correspond to exceptional points in complex momentum space, while corner zero modes emerge from exceptional curves obtained by complexifying both momenta. Compact localized states arise when the exceptional roots collapse to the origin. This framework provides a unified complex-momentum description of edge, corner, and compact localization.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that weak topology can be understood geometrically through exceptional singularities in complex momentum space, using a 2D plaquette chiral model to unify edge states, corner modes, and compact localized states under a single complex-momentum framework.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified geometric formulation of weak topology in terms of exceptional singularities, bridging the gap between weak topological invariants and localization phenomena (edge, corner, compact states).
AI.method: The authors introduce a general plaquette chiral model in 2D as a minimal realization of dual weak topology, analytically continue the Bloch Hamiltonian to complex momenta, and analyze exceptional points and curves to characterize weak topological invariants and localized states.
AI.result: Two independent families of weak topological invariants (one per spatial direction) are identified. Weak-topological edge states correspond to exceptional points in complex momentum space; corner zero modes arise from exceptional curves; compact localized states emerge when exceptional roots collapse to the origin.
AI.conclusion: The complex-momentum approach provides a unified description connecting edge, corner, and compact localization within weak topological phases.

title: Polaritons of inherently interacting molecules
summary: We investigate the absorption spectra of molecular ensembles strongly coupled to a Fabry-Pérot cavity and establish the microscopic origin of collective polaritonic bands. We show that long-range intermolecular interactions generate a large manifold of hybrid molecular-photonic states, even without disorder, vibrations, or thermal effects. The observed polariton bands are collective envelopes of these microscopic states, making photonic and molecular spectra strongly dependent on molecular arrangement. Our findings identify long-range intermolecular interactions as a key ingredient of molecular cavity QED.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that long-range intermolecular interactions, rather than disorder or vibrations, create a manifold of hybrid molecular-photonic states that collectively form polariton bands in molecular ensembles strongly coupled to optical cavities, making spectra highly sensitive to molecular arrangement.
AI.motivation: To understand the microscopic origin of collective polaritonic bands in molecular cavity QED, beyond common explanations involving disorder, vibrations, or thermal effects.
AI.method: Theoretical investigation of absorption spectra of molecular ensembles strongly coupled to a Fabry-Pérot cavity, analyzing the role of long-range intermolecular interactions in generating hybrid molecular-photonic states.
AI.result: Long-range intermolecular interactions generate a large manifold of hybrid molecular-photonic states even without disorder, vibrations, or thermal effects; polariton bands are collective envelopes of these microscopic states, causing strong dependence of spectra on molecular arrangement.
AI.conclusion: Long-range intermolecular interactions are identified as a key ingredient of molecular cavity QED, fundamentally shaping polariton band structure.

title: Photo-induced currents and short-term memory for reservoir computing in a ferroelectric semiconductor
comment: 11 pages, 4 main text figures and 3 appendix figures
summary: Physical reservoir computing represents an energy efficient approach for processing temporal signals by exploiting the intrinsic nonlinear dynamics and fading memory of a physical system. Recently, ferroelectric semiconductors moved into focus as reservoir materials motivated by their versatile electronic responses to external stimuli. Here, we explore the fundamental possibility to recognize time-varying light pulses via photo-induced currents, using the small-band-gap p-type semiconductor ErMnO$_3$ as a model system. Under white light illumination, ErMnO$_3$ exhibits non-linearly evolving photo-induced currents and controllable relaxation dynamics that naturally realize the high-dimensional projection and fading memory capabilities required for reservoir computing. The reservoir capability of ErMnO$_3$ is reflected by the improved recognition accuracy of "Past" input pulses, which increases from ~33% to ~93% after applying reservoir transformation to the input signal. The results present ferroelectric hexagonal manganites as a promising platform for photo-induced current-based reservoir computing and highlight the potential of light-driven oxide semiconductors for temporal information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the ferroelectric semiconductor ErMnO₃ can serve as a physical reservoir for recognizing time-varying light pulses via photo-induced currents, achieving a recognition accuracy improvement from ~33% to ~93% for "Past" input pulses through its nonlinear dynamics and fading memory.
AI.motivation: To explore the fundamental possibility of using photo-induced currents in ferroelectric semiconductors (specifically ErMnO₃) for temporal information processing via physical reservoir computing, offering an energy-efficient alternative to conventional computing.
AI.method: Using the small-band-gap p-type semiconductor ErMnO₃ as a model system under white light illumination, leveraging its nonlinearly evolving photo-induced currents and controllable relaxation dynamics to realize the high-dimensional projection and fading memory required for reservoir computing.
AI.result: Recognition accuracy of "Past" input pulses improved from ~33% to ~93% after applying reservoir transformation to the input signal.
AI.conclusion: Ferroelectric hexagonal manganites are a promising platform for photo-induced current-based reservoir computing, and light-driven oxide semiconductors have potential for temporal information processing.

title: Shiba duality and $η$-altermagnetism: Pairing and charge orders in bipartite attractive Hubbard models
summary: We show that Shiba duality maps the altermagnetic principle of momentum-dependent band splitting from spin to $η$-pseudospin, defining $η$-altermagnetism ($η$-ALM) as a Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) counterpart of ALM in pairing and charge orders. In half-filled pure Hubbard models on bipartite lattices, the duality relates repulsion-driven antiferromagnetism (AFM) to attraction-driven $η$-AFM with uniform singlet pairing and staggered charge-density modulation. In the BdG bands, the Shiba-dual parity-time-reversal $\mathcal{\tilde{P}}\mathcal{\tilde{T}}$ symmetry protects a Kramers degeneracy of $η$-pseudospin. Anisotropic second-neighbor hopping breaks this degeneracy and generates $η$-ALM. Odd-parity $η$-ALM shows $η$-pseudospin splitting, whereas even-parity $η$-ALM has spin-$η$-locked splitting. Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov computations on checkerboard and honeycomb lattices find $η$-ALMs with $p$-, $d$-, and $f$-wave splitting structures. Possible generalizations and experimental probes are discussed.

AI.tldr: Shiba duality extends altermagnetism from spin to η-pseudospin, defining η-altermagnetism (η-ALM) as a BdG counterpart in pairing and charge orders. Using anisotropic hopping on bipartite lattices, η-ALM exhibits p-, d-, and f-wave pseudospin splitting, with potential experimental probes.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to generalize the concept of altermagnetism—originally defined for spin splitting in momentum space—to the η-pseudospin sector via Shiba duality, thereby bridging altermagnetism with pairing and charge-density-wave orders in strongly correlated systems.
AI.method: The authors employ Shiba duality to map spin-based altermagnetism to η-pseudospin counterparts in Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) formalism. They analyze half-filled Hubbard models on bipartite lattices, identify symmetry protections (𝒫̃𝒯̃), break them with anisotropic second-neighbor hopping, and perform Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov computations on checkerboard and honeycomb lattices.
AI.result: η-ALM emerges with odd-parity (η-pseudospin splitting) and even-parity (spin-η-locked splitting) variants. Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov calculations reveal p-, d-, and f-wave splitting structures on checkerboard and honeycomb lattices.
AI.conclusion: Shiba duality provides a systematic route to realize altermagnetism in the pairing and charge order sector (η-ALM), generalizing the altermagnetic principle beyond spin. Possible experimental probes and further generalizations are discussed.

title: Emergent ferromagnetism in the NiI$_2$-NbSe$_2$ van der Waals heterostructure
summary: Multiferroicity arising from non-collinear spin textures and strong spin-orbit interactions offers a route to magnetoelectric functionality in the monolayer limit. Although theory predicts that the properties of monolayer multiferroics can be tuned by strain, gating, or proximity effects, experimental demonstrations of such control remain scarce. Here we show that the magnetic ground state of monolayer NiI$_2$, a prototypical two-dimensional multiferroic, is altered by proximity to a superconducting NbSe$_2$ substrate. Using low-temperature scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS), we show that the metallic substrate renormalizes the exchange interactions within NiI$_2$ and drives it into a ferromagnetic ground state. This can be visualized by probing the Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states within the superconducting gap of the NbSe$_2$ substrate. Our results establish YSR states as an in situ probe of two-dimensional magnetism and demonstrate substrate engineering as a means of controlling magnetic order in atomically thin materials.

AI.tldr: Monolayer NiI₂, a 2D multiferroic, undergoes a magnetic ground state transition from non-collinear to ferromagnetic when placed on a superconducting NbSe₂ substrate, as revealed by YSR states in STM/STS, demonstrating substrate engineering of 2D magnetism.
AI.motivation: While theory predicts tunability of monolayer multiferroics via strain, gating, or proximity, experimental demonstrations remain scarce. This work aims to experimentally demonstrate such control.
AI.method: Low-temperature scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS) were used to probe monolayer NiI₂ on a superconducting NbSe₂ substrate, with Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states serving as an in situ probe of the magnetic ground state.
AI.result: The NbSe₂ substrate renormalizes exchange interactions in NiI₂, driving it from a non-collinear multiferroic state into a ferromagnetic ground state, visualized via YSR states within the superconducting gap.
AI.conclusion: YSR states are established as an in situ probe of 2D magnetism, and substrate engineering is demonstrated as a viable method for controlling magnetic order in atomically thin multiferroic materials.

title: Thermal Hall Resistivity as a Unifying Description of Phonon Thermal Hall Effect in Various Insulators
summary: A considerable phonon thermal Hall effect was recently discovered across a diverse collection of materials. To clarify this enigmatic thermal Hall response in various insulators, we investigate the doped Mott insulator La$_{5/3}$Sr$_{1/3}$NiO$_4$ as an example material system and reveal a characteristic phonon-dominated thermal Hall effect. As a sensitive probe of the transverse thermal response, the thermal Hall resistivity $w_{xy}$ exhibits an insulating-like temperature dependence $w_{xy}(T)$, a linear magnetic-field dependence $w_{xy}(H)$ near $H=0$, and a $T$-linear thermal Hall angle at low temperatures. The presence of similar phenomena across a series of insulators suggests that $w_{xy}$ serves as a unifying description of phonon thermal Hall effect, corroborated by an apparent correlation between the insulating-like $w_{xy}(T)$ and material's localized electronic state.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the phonon thermal Hall effect in the doped Mott insulator La₅/₃Sr₁/₃NiO₄, finding characteristic signatures including insulating-like temperature dependence, linear magnetic-field dependence, and T-linear thermal Hall angle. These features are observed across multiple insulators, suggesting a unifying description of the phonon thermal Hall effect correlated with localized electronic states.
AI.motivation: To clarify the enigmatic phonon thermal Hall effect observed across diverse insulating materials by systematically studying a model system.
AI.method: Measurements of thermal Hall resistivity w_xy, its temperature and magnetic-field dependence, and thermal Hall angle in the doped Mott insulator La₅/₃Sr₁/₃NiO₄.
AI.result: w_xy shows insulating-like temperature dependence, linear H-dependence near zero field, and T-linear thermal Hall angle at low temperatures. Similar behavior appears across a series of insulators.
AI.conclusion: w_xy provides a unifying description of the phonon thermal Hall effect, correlated with materials' localized electronic states.

title: Towards more accurate natural orbital functional approximations: including 4-index cumulant contributions
summary: Accurate modeling of bond breaking remains a central challenge for reduced density matrix functional theory (RDMFT). Although some modern functionals can yield reasonably accurate dissociation energies, they often fail to reproduce key properties of the dissociated fragments, such as a vanishing fragment population covariance (also known as the delocalization index) and the correct total spin angular momentum of each fragment (local spin). In this work, we revisit the construction of natural orbital functionals by correcting the cumulant contribution produced by the PNOF5 functional. Our method enforces known contributions of the cumulant to local spin fragments and the delocalization index at the dissociation limit. We obtain the closest cumulant consistent with these physically motivated constraints and subsequently purify the corresponding one- and two-electron reduced density matrices by imposing the standard $P, Q, \text{and } G$ $N$-representability conditions. The resulting functional yields improved behavior in strongly correlated regimes. Benchmarking on the dissociation of the singlet states of \ce{N2}, \ce{NO+}, \ce{O2}, \ce{S2}, and \ce{CO} shows that in the dissociation regime the energies computed from the updated cumulant exactly reproduce the complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF) energies. We further analyze the limitations of the approach and identify scenarios in which the current approach performs poorly. This work provides a pathway for systematically improving natural orbital functionals to achieve reliable bond-breaking calculations within RDMFT.

AI.tldr: The paper corrects the PNOF5 functional's cumulant in RDMFT to enforce correct fragment population covariance and local spin at dissociation, yielding CASSCF-matching energies for several diatomic molecules.
AI.motivation: RDMFT struggles with bond breaking: existing functionals yield poor fragment properties (vanishing population covariance and correct local spin). The authors aim to fix this by correcting the cumulant contribution.
AI.method: The authors revisit natural orbital functional construction by correcting the cumulant from PNOF5, enforcing physically motivated constraints on local spin and delocalization index at dissociation, then purifying the 1- and 2-RDMs via P, Q, G N-representability conditions.
AI.result: For N2, NO+, O2, S2, and CO singlet dissociations, the updated cumulant yields energies matching CASSCF in the dissociation regime. Limitations are identified for scenarios where the approach performs poorly.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a systematic pathway for improving natural orbital functionals to achieve reliable bond-breaking calculations within RDMFT.

title: MatDiffract: A Material-Informed Automated Analysis Platform for X-ray Powder Diffraction
summary: High-throughput experimentation and self-driving laboratories are drastically accelerating materials discovery, yet automated interpretation of X-ray powder diffraction (XRPD) data remains a critical rate-limiting step. Conventional search-match workflows rely heavily on expert manual intervention, while pure data-driven machine learning approaches suffer from limited generalizability across chemical systems and lack rigorous crystallographic interpretability. Here we present MatDiffract, a material-informed automated analysis platform for high-throughput XRPD characterization. Built on a first-principles density functional theory (DFT)-derived inorganic crystal structure database, Atomly, MatDiffract constructs a perturbation-augmented simulated diffraction database, embeds multi-scale diffraction features into indexable vectors, and integrates hierarchical vector retrieval with full-pattern fitting Rietveld refinement and quantitative phase fitting. Benchmarked on 875 single-phase experimental patterns, the platform achieves 91.3% Top-1 and 97.2% Top-10 identification accuracy after automated refinement. For binary and ternary multiphase mixtures, it delivers 85.0% and 70.0% Top-1 accuracy with mass fraction mean absolute errors as low as 1.2% and 1.8%, respectively. Beyond mere phase labeling, MatDiffract outputs full crystallographic results including refined structural models, fitted profiles, and quantitative compositions within tens of seconds per sample. Its modular vector-based architecture supports seamless incremental expansion to new material systems, providing an end-to-end solution to close the characterization throughput gap for autonomous materials discovery and high-throughput materials development.

AI.tldr: MatDiffract is an automated XRPD analysis platform that combines DFT-derived simulated diffraction databases, hierarchical vector retrieval, and Rietveld refinement to achieve high-accuracy phase identification (91.3% Top-1 for single-phase) and quantitative analysis for multiphase mixtures, outputting full crystallographic results in tens of seconds.
AI.motivation: Automated XRPD data interpretation is a critical bottleneck in high-throughput materials discovery; conventional methods need manual intervention and ML approaches lack generalizability and crystallographic interpretability.
AI.method: Built on the Atomly DFT-derived crystal structure database, MatDiffract constructs a perturbation-augmented simulated diffraction database, embeds multi-scale diffraction features into indexable vectors, and integrates hierarchical vector retrieval with full-pattern fitting Rietveld refinement and quantitative phase fitting.
AI.result: On 875 single-phase patterns: 91.3% Top-1 and 97.2% Top-10 accuracy. For binary/ternary mixtures: 85.0%/70.0% Top-1 accuracy with mass fraction MAE of 1.2%/1.8%.
AI.conclusion: MatDiffract provides an end-to-end, modular, and extensible solution that closes the characterization throughput gap for autonomous materials discovery and high-throughput materials development.

title: Circular phonon dichroism in $d$-wave altermagnets
summary: Altermagnets, a new class of collinear antiferromagnets, exhibit momentum-dependent spin splitting and offer compelling advantages for antiferromagnetic spintronics. However, the magnetic order is intrinsically difficult to read out, which hinders practical applications. We propose finite-momentum circular phonon dichroism as a direct probe of Néel vector in two-dimensional $d$-wave altermagnets. Combining Onsager reciprocity with $C_{2z}$ lattice symmetry, we find that the dichroic signal reverses sign when the Néel vector is flipped for the in-plane phonon wave vectors. Moreover, a channel-resolved decomposition identifies the circular phonon dichroism originates from the interband coherent transitions. Representative finite-momentum cuts show pronounced dichroic asymmetric ratio, with $|η_{\mathrm{CPD}}|=37.3\%$. Our work reveals that the circular-ultrasound absorption acts as a direct probe of the Néel vector of $d$-wave altermagnets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using finite-momentum circular phonon dichroism as a direct optical probe to read out the Néel vector in 2D d-wave altermagnets, achieving up to 37.3% dichroic asymmetry.
AI.motivation: Altermagnets offer advantages for antiferromagnetic spintronics, but their magnetic order (Néel vector) is intrinsically difficult to read out, hindering practical applications.
AI.method: The authors combine Onsager reciprocity with C₂z lattice symmetry to show that the circular phonon dichroism signal reverses sign upon Néel vector flipping. They perform channel-resolved decomposition to attribute the effect to interband coherent transitions.
AI.result: The dichroic asymmetric ratio reaches |η_CPD| = 37.3% at representative finite-momentum cuts, confirming strong and detectable signal contrast.
AI.conclusion: Circular-ultrasound absorption serves as a direct, symmetry-based probe of the Néel vector in d-wave altermagnets, enabling readout for antiferromagnetic spintronics.

title: Approximating committor functions: Objective functions and training data sampling
comment: 37 ages in the main text with 9 Figures and 8 pages in the supplementary material
summary: Many molecular dynamics simulations aim at studying transitions between two states (from reactants to products). In this context, the committor function (which gives for a given molecular configuration the probability to reach the product state before the reactant state) is a pivotal quantity, in particular because it is the optimal importance function for rare event simulation methods such as importance sampling or splitting techniques. These methods are used to sample the reactive path ensemble, and estimate for example the transition rate. However, learning such a function is generally a challenging task due to the high dimensionality of the configuration space. In this work, after reviewing the existing methodologies to construct approximate committor functions, a new loss function based on the application of Itō's formula is proposed to learn the committor function with a minimization procedure on the parameters of a neural network. After comparing this novel approach to existing procedures on the Müller--Brown potential, we introduce a coupling strategy with the Adaptive Multilevel Splitting method to better approximate the committor function using a better sampling of the reactive trajectories. This methodology in which the committor function is iteratively learned only requires initially the knowledge of the reactant and product states.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new loss function based on Itō's formula to learn the committor function via neural network minimization, and couples it with Adaptive Multilevel Splitting (AMS) to iteratively improve the approximation using reactive trajectory sampling.
AI.motivation: The committor function is crucial for rare event simulation methods (importance sampling, splitting) but is difficult to learn due to the high dimensionality of molecular configuration space.
AI.method: A novel loss function derived from Itō's formula is used to train a neural network to approximate the committor function. This is coupled with Adaptive Multilevel Splitting (AMS) to iteratively refine the approximation by improving the sampling of reactive trajectories.
AI.result: The new approach is compared with existing methods on the Müller-Brown potential, demonstrating its effectiveness. The coupling with AMS enables iterative learning of the committor function using only knowledge of reactant and product states.
AI.conclusion: The proposed methodology provides a way to approximate the committor function in high-dimensional spaces with minimal prior information (only reactant/product states), enabling more efficient rare event simulations.

title: Long- and Short-Range Anion Order in SrTiO$_{3-x}$H$_x$ Perovskite Oxyhydrides: DFT+$U$ Sensitivity and HSE06 Cluster Expansion
summary: Anion ordering in perovskite oxyhydrides can remain significant even in disordered states, particularly at non-dilute hydrogen concentrations. Nevertheless, hydride substitution poses challenges for accurate simulations based on density functional theory due to configurational complexity and Ti 3$d$ reduction. Here, we develop a cluster expansion (CE) framework for SrTiO$_{3-x}$H$_x$ incorporating HSE06 hybrid-DFT energetics. We first demonstrate that calculated mixing energies and ordering stability are highly sensitive to the choice of DFT+$U$, with maximum variations on the order of 100 meV/anion. We benchmark ordering energetics against HSE06 calculations and identify $U$ = 3.3 eV as an HSE06 proxy, which enables extensive configurational exploration while limiting costly HSE06 calculations to key configurations for efficient learning of ordering energetics. Together, ground-state orderings, correlations between octahedral configurations and structural stability, and MC sampling of CE models all support a strong preference for the O$_4$H$_2$ cis configuration in SrTiO$_{3-x}$H$_x$, in which two hydride ions occupy first-nearest-neighbor anion sites. This cis-type preference was overlooked in previous ATiO$_{3-x}$H$_x$ studies, despite its sizable stabilization of ~200 meV per hydride comparable to reported anion-migration and polaron-formation energies. This study addresses both the previously underexplored sensitivity of CE-based ordering analyses to DFT+$U$ and anion-ordering in perovskite oxyhydrides.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a cluster expansion framework for SrTiO₃₋ₓHₓ using HSE06 hybrid-DFT, revealing that DFT+U choice significantly impacts ordering energetics (up to ~100 meV/anion), identifies U=3.3 eV as an optimal HSE06 proxy, and discovers a strong preference for the O₄H₂ cis configuration—overlooked in previous studies—with ~200 meV/hydride stabilization energy.
AI.motivation: To address the challenges in simulating perovskite oxyhydrides with non-dilute hydrogen concentrations, where anion ordering remains significant even in disordered states, and where standard DFT+U methods show high sensitivity to model parameters, leading to unreliable configurational energetics.
AI.method: Developed a cluster expansion (CE) framework incorporating HSE06 hybrid-DFT as reference; benchmarked DFT+U against HSE06 to identify U=3.3 eV as an optimal proxy; combined ground-state ordering analysis, octahedral configuration-structure correlations, and Monte Carlo sampling of CE models.
AI.result: DFT+U mixing energies vary by up to ~100 meV/anion depending on U choice; U=3.3 eV best reproduces HSE06 ordering energetics; the O₄H₂ cis configuration is strongly favored (~200 meV/hydride stabilization), which was missed in prior ATiO₃₋ₓHₓ studies.
AI.conclusion: The cis-type hydride ordering preference in SrTiO₃₋ₓHₓ is energetically significant (comparable to anion-migration and polaron-formation energies) and highlights the sensitivity of CE-based ordering analyses to the underlying DFT functional, necessitating careful benchmark against hybrid functionals.

title: Direct Measurement of Exciton Dispersion in the Long-Wavelength Limit
summary: Exciton dispersion, which governs the propagation, scattering and radiative decay of electron-hole pairs, is essential to optoelectronics and quantum materials. In two-dimensional systems, weakened dielectric screening and long-range electron-hole exchange are predicted to induce nonanalytic exciton dispersion in the long-wavelength limit. However, direct quantitative characterization of its dimensional evolution remains lacking, especially in the ultralow-q regime (q < 0.02 $Å^{-1}$). Here we employ defocus-engineered momentum-resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy in scanning transmission electron microscopy, achieving an ultrahigh momentum resolution of 0.0002 $Å^{-1}$. Using freestanding hBN as a prototypical platform, we resolve layer-dependent exciton dispersion and quantify its characteristic crossover momentum and group velocity in the long-wavelength limit. With increasing thickness, the nonanalytic linear-dispersion regime is progressively compressed, manifested by a reduction in characteristic crossover momentum q_c from $1.82 \times 10^{-1} Å^{-1}$ in the monolayer to $3.0 \times 10^{-1} Å^{-1}$ in 25 layers. Meanwhile, the low-q group velocity increases from $2.0 \times 10^{-3} c$ to $2.9 \times 10^{-2} c$, before the dispersion ultimately approaches the bulk-like parabolic limit. We further examine how the exciton band structure of monolayer hBN responds to its surrounding environment, including temperature, adjacent graphene layers, and interlayer twist in BN/graphene heterostructures. These findings uncover the fundamental physics of low-dimensional excitons, deliver valuable guidance for modulating exciton transport, diffusion and quasiparticle coupling in layered quantum materials, and establish a powerful experimental route to explore low-dimensional exciton physics.

AI.tldr: Using momentum-resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy with ultrahigh momentum resolution (0.0002 Å⁻¹), this study directly measures layer-dependent exciton dispersion in freestanding hBN, revealing that nonanalytic linear dispersion is progressively compressed with increasing thickness, with crossover momentum q_c shifting from 1.82×10⁻¹ Å⁻¹ (monolayer) to 3.0×10⁻¹ Å⁻¹ (25 layers) and group velocity increasing from 2.0×10⁻³ c to 2.9×10⁻² c as the dispersion approaches the bulk parabolic limit. Environmental effects (temperature, graphene adjacency, interlayer twist) are also examined.
AI.motivation: To directly and quantitatively characterize exciton dispersion in two-dimensional systems, particularly in the ultralow-q regime (q < 0.02 Å⁻¹), where nonanalytic behavior is predicted but has remained experimentally elusive due to insufficient momentum resolution.
AI.method: Defocus-engineered momentum-resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) in scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), achieving an ultrahigh momentum resolution of 0.0002 Å⁻¹, applied to freestanding hBN layers of varying thickness.
AI.result: Layer-dependent nonanalytic linear-dispersion regime compression: q_c increases from 1.82×10⁻¹ Å⁻¹ (monolayer) to 3.0×10⁻¹ Å⁻¹ (25 layers); low-q group velocity increases from 2.0×10⁻³ c to 2.9×10⁻² c; dispersion evolves toward bulk-like parabolic limit with thickness.
AI.conclusion: These findings uncover fundamental low-dimensional exciton physics, provide guidance for modulating exciton transport and quasiparticle coupling in layered quantum materials, and establish a powerful experimental route for exploring low-dimensional exciton dispersion.

title: Axel Dieter Becke: Not just the "B" in "B3LYP"
comment: Prepared for the journal Electronic Structure volume focusing on Axel Becke https://iopscience.iop.org/collections/est-260317-1076
summary: There is hardly anyone doing electronic structure calculations on molecules who has not used the famous B3LYP functional. Many will even know that the "B" in B3LYP stands for Becke, but how many know the history of the B3LYP functional? Behind this functional, Axel Becke has two of the most highly cited papers in both chemistry and physics---both with several tens of thousands of citations---and many less cited, but arguably equally important accomplishments, that led to B3LYP, as well as continued developments in building ever better density-functional approximatons after the appearance of B3LYP. Axel has received much recognition and many honors for his work. In particular, in 2015, Axel was awarded Canada's highest honor for science and engineering---namely the Gerhard Herzberg Gold Medal. Achievements like this require more than "just" brilliance; they require being the right person in the right place at the right time. I will argue that Axel did indeed fulfill these requirements. At the same time, I will try to give some flavor of the field of electronic structure as seen through my own eyes and those of a few others during the period from the beginning of Axel's career up until very recent times.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a historical perspective on Axel Becke's contributions to density functional theory, particularly the development of the B3LYP functional, which is one of the most widely used methods in electronic structure calculations. It traces Becke's career from his early highly-cited papers through his continued work on density-functional approximations, culminating in his receiving the Gerhard Herzberg Gold Medal in 2015.
AI.motivation: To document and celebrate the historical significance of Axel Becke's work in developing the B3LYP functional and advancing density functional theory, while providing personal and professional context for how his achievements unfolded.
AI.method: Historical narrative and personal perspective, drawing on the author's own observations and those of a few colleagues, tracing Becke's career from its beginning to recent times.
AI.result: The B3LYP functional became ubiquitous in electronic structure calculations; Becke's two most highly cited papers in chemistry and physics each have tens of thousands of citations; Becke received the Gerhard Herzberg Gold Medal (Canada's highest science and engineering honor) in 2015.
