AI.conclusion: Becke's success with B3LYP and subsequent developments resulted from a combination of brilliance, being the right person in the right place at the right time, and continued effort to improve density-functional approximations even after B3LYP's widespread adoption.

title: Orbital Hall Effect Enables Field-Free Magnetization Reversal in Ferrimagnets without Additional Conversion Layer
summary: The spin Hall effect provides a well-established route for electrical magnetization control, while the orbital Hall effect offers a powerful yet less explored source of angular momentum. Achieving field-free deterministic switching in straightforward orbital-torque architectures remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate orbital-Hall-current-driven switching in a Mo/CoGd bilayer without the need for a separate orbital-to-spin conversion layer across a wide temperature range. In this simplified geometry, Mo serves as both an orbital and spin current source. However, the spin contribution is insufficient due to weak spin-orbit coupling, which is consistent with first-principles calculations predicting a large orbital Hall conductivity. The adjacent ferrimagnetic CoGd layer provides both orbital-to-spin conversion and the perpendicular switching medium. Planar Hall and current-induced loop-shift measurements reveal a substantial unconventional z-polarized damping-like torque originating from interfacial symmetry breaking. Increasing the Mo thickness from 0.2 to 2 nm increases torque efficiency by approximately 31% (y-polarized) and 71% (z-polarized) components. This enhancement enables field-free deterministic switching with a critical current density down to 2.51 x 10^6 A cm^-2. Our results establish Mo/CoGd bilayers as a compact platform for orbital-current switching and point toward low-power orbitronic memory devices.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates field-free deterministic switching in Mo/CoGd bilayers driven by orbital Hall current without a separate orbital-to-spin conversion layer, enabled by large orbital Hall conductivity in Mo and interfacial symmetry breaking in the ferrimagnetic CoGd layer, achieving low critical current density of 2.51 × 10^6 A cm^-2.
AI.motivation: While the spin Hall effect is well-established for magnetization control, the orbital Hall effect offers a powerful but less explored angular momentum source. Achieving field-free deterministic switching in simple orbital-torque architectures remains challenging, motivating the search for a compact platform.
AI.method: Mo/CoGd bilayer structure is used where Mo acts as both orbital and spin current source (with spin contribution insufficient due to weak spin-orbit coupling, confirmed by first-principles calculations showing large orbital Hall conductivity). CoGd serves as both orbital-to-spin conversion layer and perpendicular switching medium. Planar Hall and current-induced loop-shift measurements characterize torque components.
AI.result: Unconventional z-polarized damping-like torque arises from interfacial symmetry breaking. Increasing Mo thickness from 0.2 to 2 nm enhances torque efficiency by ~31% (y-polarized) and ~71% (z-polarized), enabling field-free deterministic switching with critical current density down to 2.51 × 10^6 A cm^-2 across a wide temperature range.
AI.conclusion: Mo/CoGd bilayers provide a compact platform for orbital-current switching, pointing toward low-power orbitronic memory devices.

title: Visualization of Defect Electronic States in Layered Semiconductor CrSBr
summary: Chromium sulfur bromide (CrSBr) is a layered magnetic semiconducting material combining a rich magnetic phase diagram with axis-dependent electronic and optical properties. While defects in CrSBr have been shown to affect magnetic order and excitonic responses, their microscopic nature, atomic structure, and electronic properties are not yet fully understood. In this work, we use scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS) to explore the structure and electronic signatures of two prominent defects in bulk CrSBr. Their structure reflects the symmetries of the underlying lattice, with electronic features near the valence band edge. By comparing experimental data with ab initio simulated STM images, we infer that a common defect corresponds to a b-axis-aligned double sulfur vacancy, in line with findings from a recent growth analysis study. This result advances our understanding of the role of intrinsic defects in shaping the electronic structure of CrSBr.

AI.tldr: This paper uses STM/STS and ab initio simulations to identify a common defect in CrSBr as a b-axis-aligned double sulfur vacancy, revealing its structure and electronic signatures near the valence band edge.
AI.motivation: Defects in CrSBr are known to affect magnetic order and excitonic responses, but their microscopic nature, atomic structure, and electronic properties remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS) combined with ab initio simulated STM images to explore defect structures and electronic signatures.
AI.result: The identified common defect is a b-axis-aligned double sulfur vacancy, consistent with recent growth analysis findings, and its structure reflects the symmetries of the underlying lattice with electronic features near the valence band edge.
AI.conclusion: This work advances the understanding of intrinsic defects and their role in shaping the electronic structure of CrSBr.

title: Interlayer interactions reshape charge-density wave through electronic elasticity in 4H$_{\mathrm{b}}$-TaS$_2$
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, includes 11 pages supplementary and 7 supplementary figures
summary: Incommensurate charge-density waves (CDWs) in layered quantum materials frequently exhibit widely varying ordering wave vectors, even among nominally identical samples, obscuring their intrinsic electronic properties. Here we identify an inherent origin of this variability through the electronic elasticity of an incommensurate CDW using the model heterostructure 4H$_{\mathrm{b}}$-TaS$_2$, composed of alternating commensurate CDW on 1T and incommensurate CDW on 1H layers. Low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy, combined with Fourier and quasiparticle-interference analysis, exploits the lattice-pinned 1T CDW as an internal reference to resolve discrete compressive ($-2.3\%$) and tensile ($+3.2\%$) elastic states of the neighboring 1H CDW selected by the interlayer registry of the adjacent layers. Corresponding few-meV shifts of a flat band demonstrate that weak interlayer interactions reshape the low-energy electronic structure through the intrinsic elasticity of the incommensurate CDW. These findings establish electronic elasticity as a mechanism by which subtle interlayer interactions control correlated electronic states in van der Waals heterostructures.

AI.tldr: Using 4Hb-TaS2 as a model system, the paper shows that the ordering wave vector variability in incommensurate CDWs arises from intrinsic electronic elasticity, where interlayer registry selects discrete compressive (−2.3%) or tensile (+3.2%) elastic states of the CDW, leading to few-meV shifts in flat bands and thereby controlling low-energy electronic structure in van der Waals heterostructures.
AI.motivation: Incommensurate CDWs in layered quantum materials exhibit widely varying ordering wave vectors even among nominally identical samples, obscuring their intrinsic electronic properties. The authors aim to identify the inherent origin of this variability.
AI.method: Low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy combined with Fourier and quasiparticle-interference analysis, using the lattice-pinned 1T CDW as an internal reference in the 4Hb-TaS2 heterostructure.
AI.result: Discrete compressive (−2.3%) and tensile (+3.2%) elastic states of the 1H CDW are selected by interlayer registry, with corresponding few-meV shifts of a flat band.
AI.conclusion: Electronic elasticity is a mechanism by which subtle interlayer interactions control correlated electronic states in van der Waals heterostructures.

title: First-Principles Analysis of Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity at Molecule-Metal Interfaces in Photoemission
summary: Spin-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (PES) probes chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS), yet it remains unclear whether the measured spin polarization reflects molecular chirality itself or the broader electronic structure of the hybrid interface. We present a first-principles analysis of PES spin polarization at chiral molecule-metal interfaces, treating the interface holistically rather than as a metal substrate plus a separate molecular spin filter/polarizer. Using density functional theory within a three-step photoemission framework, we compute the spin polarization generated in the optical-excitation step for ($M$)- and ($P$)-heptahelicene adsorbed on Au(111) and Cu(111), and for coronene/Au(111) as a non-chiral control. We find that adsorption strongly reshapes the PES spin polarization relative to the clean metal surface, but opposite enantiomers yield symmetry-related responses. These results indicate that changes in the PES spin polarization are more naturally attributed to the electronic structure of the hybrid interface than to molecular chirality alone.

AI.tldr: First-principles analysis shows that spin polarization in photoelectron spectroscopy at chiral molecule-metal interfaces reflects the hybrid interface's electronic structure rather than molecular chirality alone.
AI.motivation: To resolve whether spin polarization measured in spin-resolved PES of chiral molecule-metal interfaces originates from molecular chirality itself or the broader electronic structure of the hybrid interface.
AI.method: First-principles density functional theory within a three-step photoemission framework, computing spin polarization in the optical-excitation step for (M)- and (P)-heptahelicene on Au(111) and Cu(111), with coronene/Au(111) as a non-chiral control.
AI.result: Adsorption strongly reshapes PES spin polarization relative to clean metal surfaces; opposite enantiomers yield symmetry-related responses. The non-chiral control also shows spin polarization changes, indicating the effect is not exclusively chirality-driven.
AI.conclusion: Changes in PES spin polarization are more naturally attributed to the electronic structure of the hybrid interface than to molecular chirality alone.

title: Visualizing Microwave-Driven Dynamics of Antiskyrmions and Surface Skyrmions
summary: Microwaves provide coherent access to low-energy excitations and serve as effective probes of high-frequency spin dynamics in quantum and magnetic systems. For topological spin textures, microwave excitation is expected to generate rich collective responses, yet direct real-space observation of ultrafast dynamics remains limited. Here we use time-resolved Lorentz transmission electron microscopy to visualize microwave-driven dynamics in a hybrid antiskyrmion structure composed of a central antiskyrmion and surface skyrmions. We resolve the picosecond evolution of antiskyrmion area and second-harmonic signals, evidencing nonlinear responses of spin textures under microwave excitations. We track the core motions of the antiskyrmion and surface skyrmions, which follow distinct trajectories while sharing the same rotational sense. Micromagnetic simulations reproduce the key observations and associate the dynamic modes with the spatial modulation of the core profile along the thickness. These achievements establish ultrafast electron microscopy as a powerful real-space approach for probing high-frequency microwave-driven dynamics of topological magnetic solitons.

AI.tldr: Researchers used time-resolved Lorentz transmission electron microscopy to directly visualize microwave-driven ultrafast dynamics of hybrid antiskyrmion structures, revealing picosecond evolution, nonlinear responses, and distinct core motions, establishing real-space ultrafast electron microscopy for probing topological magnetic soliton dynamics.
AI.motivation: Microwave excitation of topological spin textures is expected to generate rich collective responses, but direct real-space observation of their ultrafast dynamics has remained limited.
AI.method: Time-resolved Lorentz transmission electron microscopy combined with micromagnetic simulations to visualize microwave-driven dynamics in hybrid antiskyrmion structures.
AI.result: Resolved picosecond evolution of antiskyrmion area and second-harmonic signals, demonstrating nonlinear responses; tracked core motions of antiskyrmion and surface skyrmions showing distinct trajectories with shared rotational sense.
AI.conclusion: Ultrafast electron microscopy is established as a powerful real-space approach for probing high-frequency microwave-driven dynamics of topological magnetic solitons.

title: An on-chip programmable mechano-quantum transducer
summary: Solid-state spin defects encode local perturbations as measurable shifts in spin-transition frequencies, but mechanical actuation and quantum readout remain physically separated, resulting in a discrete measurement setup. Integrating these functions requires an on-site mechano-quantum interface that programs the lattice state of a defect host and quantitatively maps it onto the spin Hamiltonian. Here we first report an on-chip programmable mechano-quantum transducer (OCPMQT) that integrates voltage-defined micromechanical actuation with in situ spin-frequency readout in a two-dimensional van der Waals quantum-defect host. Mechanically programmed lattice states are encoded as shifts in the axial zero-field splitting parameter and resolved by optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectroscopy. Within a chip volume of 2.05*10^-2 cm^3, the transducer accesses ODMR-inferred strains as low as 0.0080% and delivers a volumetric force density of approximately 2.6*104 N/m^-3. A micromechanical-to-spin-Hamiltonian framework links on-chip electromechanics, interfacial strain transfer, and strain-spin coupling, enabling the electrical control micromechanical input to be measured directly as spin-frequency response.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first on-chip programmable mechano-quantum transducer (OCPMQT) that integrates micromechanical actuation with in situ spin readout in a 2D van der Waals quantum-defect host, achieving strain sensing down to 0.0080% and volumetric force density of ~2.6×10^4 N/m³ within a compact chip volume.
AI.motivation: Existing solid-state spin defect systems have mechanical actuation and quantum readout physically separated, resulting in discrete measurement setups. There is a need to integrate these functions into a unified on-chip platform that can program the lattice state of a defect host and map it onto the spin Hamiltonian quantitatively.
AI.method: The authors developed an OCPMQT that uses voltage-defined micromechanical actuation combined with in situ ODMR readout in a 2D van der Waals quantum-defect host. They established a micromechanical-to-spin-Hamiltonian framework linking on-chip electromechanics, interfacial strain transfer, and strain-spin coupling to directly measure micromechanical input as spin-frequency response.
AI.result: The transducer achieves ODMR-inferred strains as low as 0.0080% and a volumetric force density of approximately 2.6×10^4 N/m³ within a chip volume of 2.05×10^-2 cm³.
AI.conclusion: The OCPMQT successfully integrates mechanical actuation and quantum readout monolithically, providing a compact mechano-quantum interface that can directly map mechanical inputs onto spin Hamiltonian parameters, enabling future integrated quantum sensing and actuation platforms.

title: Pseudogap formation in the moderate correlated layered attractive Hubbard model
summary: We consider the layered attractive Hubbard model with a moderate interaction strength at quarter filling. The Green's function, self-energy, and density of states are calculated for relatively large clusters using the fluctuating local field method within the approximation of vanishing effective interaction. The emergence of a pseudogap is demonstrated for the cluster system, and it is shown that integration over the fluctuating field is equivalent to the summation of zero-mode ladder diagrams above critical temperature. For the large layered system, a pseudogap in the density of states is obtained within a cluster scheme that treats the coupling between layers as a static $U(1)$ symmetry-breaking field.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the layered attractive Hubbard model at quarter filling using the fluctuating local field method. It shows that a pseudogap emerges in cluster systems and that integrating over the fluctuating field sums zero-mode ladder diagrams above critical temperature. For large systems, a pseudogap is obtained by treating interlayer coupling as a static U(1) symmetry-breaking field.
AI.motivation: To understand the emergence of pseudogap in the layered attractive Hubbard model with moderate interaction strength at quarter filling, using the fluctuating local field method.
AI.method: Fluctuating local field method within the approximation of vanishing effective interaction; cluster calculations of Green's function, self-energy, and density of states; treatment of interlayer coupling as a static U(1) symmetry-breaking field for large systems.
AI.result: A pseudogap emerges in the cluster system; integration over the fluctuating field is equivalent to summation of zero-mode ladder diagrams above Tc; a pseudogap in DOS is obtained for large layered systems.
AI.conclusion: The fluctuating local field method captures pseudogap physics in the layered attractive Hubbard model, with the gap arising from pairing fluctuations and interlayer coupling effects.

title: Reconstructing local environments from concise atomistic representations
summary: Symmetry-based representations of local atomic structure, such as the power spectrum or bispectrum, are routinely used to characterize the structural diversity of datasets and as input features for atomistic machine learning. Although these descriptors systematically incorporate increasingly complex geometric correlations, it remains unclear if a given feature can be mapped back to a discrete point cloud, whether such a reconstruction is unique, and how changes in the descriptor are reflected in the underlying atomic geometry. The choice and discretization of the radial and angular bases, as well as the high dimensionality of the resulting feature vectors -- which may contain hundreds or thousands of components -- make this interpretation even more challenging. In this work, we investigate the inverse problem of recovering atomic structures from invariant descriptors. We show that accurate reconstructions can be obtained from remarkably compact descriptors of different correlation orders, each comprising only a few tens of features. Even representations that are formally incomplete or locally ill-conditioned can be inverted to accurate geometric reconstructions of atomic environments across molecular and material datasets. Our reconstruction framework provides a general algorithmic means of identifying approximate degeneracies of invariant descriptors and recovering distinct atomic environments that cannot be distinguished by a given representation. Finally, by reconstructing atomic configurations from descriptors, we examine how perturbations in invariant descriptors of different correlation orders translate into structural distortions.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that atomic structures can be accurately reconstructed from compact symmetry-invariant descriptors (e.g., power spectrum, bispectrum), even when descriptors are formally incomplete. The authors develop a reconstruction framework to probe descriptor degeneracies and understand how descriptor perturbations map to structural distortions.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether invariant descriptors of atomic structure (like power spectrum or bispectrum) can be inverted back to discrete point clouds, whether such reconstructions are unique, and how changes in descriptors relate to changes in atomic geometry. This interpretability challenge is compounded by high-dimensional feature vectors and choice of basis functions.
AI.method: The authors investigate the inverse problem of recovering atomic structures from invariant descriptors. They test reconstruction from compact descriptors of varying correlation orders, using only tens of features, across molecular and material datasets.
AI.result: Accurate reconstructions are obtainable from remarkably compact descriptors. Even formally incomplete or locally ill-conditioned representations can be inverted to accurate geometric reconstructions. The framework identifies approximate degeneracies where distinct atomic environments yield similar descriptors.
AI.conclusion: The reconstruction framework provides a general algorithmic means to identify degenerate invariant descriptors and to map perturbations in descriptor space to structural distortions in atomic geometries, enhancing interpretability of symmetry-based atomic representations.

title: Probing the nonlocality of Landau levels in GaAs quantum wells through modified Purcell factors, Lamb shifts and dipole emitted spectra
summary: In a two-dimensional electron gas, a strong perpendicular magnetic field confines electrons to quantized cyclotron orbits, giving rise to Landau levels with discrete orbit radii. Even the smallest Landau orbit, set by the magnetic length, spans tens of nanometers for fields of a few Tesla, imposing an intrinsic nonlocal response to electromagnetic excitations. From a microscopic theory of the nonlocal susceptibility, we derive the Green's function, the central quantity governing all electromagnetic interactions, and evaluate Purcell factors, Lamb shifts, and emission spectra from a proximal dipole emitter beyond the Markov and rotating-wave approximations. Significant nonlocal effects resulting from spatial dispersion of the Landau level response modify the response for experimentally relevant situations up to distances of hundreds of nanometers and, in particular, brighten locally dipole-forbidden transitions due to near-field gradients at multiples of the cyclotron frequency. The relevant length scales are typical of state-of-the-art nanostructured terahertz architectures, and some of our nonlocal features are consistent with recent experiments using Landau level polaritons.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a microscopic theory of nonlocal electromagnetic response in a two-dimensional electron gas under a strong magnetic field, deriving Green's functions to compute Purcell factors, Lamb shifts, and emission spectra beyond Markov and rotating-wave approximations. Significant nonlocal effects persist up to hundreds of nanometers and can brighten dipole-forbidden transitions at cyclotron frequency multiples.
AI.motivation: Landau levels in a 2DEG under a strong magnetic field have discrete orbit radii set by the magnetic length (tens of nanometers), imposing intrinsic nonlocal response to electromagnetic excitations that cannot be captured by local approximations.
AI.method: A microscopic theory of the nonlocal susceptibility is used to derive the Green's function governing all electromagnetic interactions. Purcell factors, Lamb shifts, and emission spectra are evaluated beyond the Markov and rotating-wave approximations.
AI.result: Nonlocal effects due to spatial dispersion of Landau level response are significant up to hundreds of nanometers, brightening locally dipole-forbidden transitions via near-field gradients at multiples of the cyclotron frequency. Results are consistent with recent experiments on Landau level polaritons.
AI.conclusion: Nonlocal corrections are essential for correctly modeling electromagnetic interactions in 2DEG systems under magnetic fields, particularly for state-of-the-art terahertz nanostructures where relevant length scales overlap.

title: Strong correlations and local self-energies from on-site ensembles
summary: Addressing the many-body electronic-structure problem is a central goal of modern condensed-matter physics. Paramagnetic Mott insulators, in particular, have long represented a challenge for standard approaches, such as density-functional theory. Historically, these systems have been tackled either by considering many-body dynamics, as in the case of dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), or, more recently, by invoking a polymorphous description consisting of large supercells populated with static symmetry-broken motifs whose spatial average restores the paramagnetic state. Inspired by these viewpoints, we introduce the on-site dephased ensemble (DE) approximation, in which the local electronic-structure problem is described by a thermal ensemble of all accessible local static solutions; this gives rise to a strong frequency dependence of the local electronic self-energy, as seen in DMFT or in the coherent-potential approximation of disordered alloys. We show that the DE successfully recovers defining hallmarks of strongly correlated Mott systems, both in terms of the self-energy as well as the persistence of local moments in time, in quantitative agreement with DMFT. By bypassing expensive quantum Monte Carlo solvers or large supercell calculations, this approach offers efficient routes to treating paramagnetic Mott systems in a first-principles setting, and highlights a deeper connection between the physics of strong correlations and that of disorder.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the on-site dephased ensemble (DE) approximation, a method that treats the local electronic structure as a thermal ensemble of static solutions to capture strong correlations in paramagnetic Mott insulators, achieving quantitative agreement with DMFT while bypassing expensive solvers or supercell calculations.
AI.motivation: Paramagnetic Mott insulators challenge standard approaches like density-functional theory; existing methods (DMFT, supercell-based polymorphous descriptions) are computationally expensive. The goal is to develop an efficient yet accurate first-principles approach to treat strongly correlated Mott systems.
AI.method: The on-site dephased ensemble (DE) approximation describes the local electronic-structure problem via a thermal ensemble of all accessible local static solutions, generating a strong frequency dependence of the local electronic self-energy, analogous to DMFT or coherent-potential approximation for disordered alloys.
AI.result: The DE successfully recovers hallmarks of strongly correlated Mott systems, including the self-energy structure and the persistence of local moments in time, in quantitative agreement with DMFT.
AI.conclusion: The DE offers efficient routes to treating paramagnetic Mott systems in a first-principles setting, bypassing expensive quantum Monte Carlo solvers or large supercell calculations, and reveals a deeper connection between strong correlations and disorder physics.

title: Lifetime effects and satellites in the photoelectron spectrum of platinum metal
summary: This work presents a comprehensive investigation of the electronic structure and many-body photoemission effects in metallic platinum using reflection high-energy electron energy-loss spec- troscopy (RHEELS), soft X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (SXPS), and hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES), supported by ab initio calculations. Shallow and deep core state spectra enable the systematic characterisation of intrinsic line-shape asymmetries and satellite structures. Correlation of photoelectron satellites with RHEELS loss features allows the assignment of inter- band transitions, surface and bulk plasmons, plasmonic overtones, and semi-core ionisation losses across the Pt spectrum. Several previously unresolved satellite features and spin-orbit splittings are identified and discussed. Comparison of experimental valence band spectra with orbital-projected densities of states calculated using ab initio density functional theory (DFT) and G0W0 approaches, with and without spin-orbit coupling, demonstrates the critical role of relativistic effects in reproducing the Pt valence electronic structure. Together, these results establish a unified, internally consistent spectroscopic reference for metallic platinum, providing a robust framework for interpreting photoelectron spectra of Pt-containing catalysts, electronic materials, and related 5d transition metal systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive spectroscopic investigation of metallic platinum using RHEELS, SXPS, HAXPES, and ab initio calculations, establishing a unified reference for line-shape asymmetries, satellite structures, plasmons, and relativistic effects in Pt electronic structure.
AI.motivation: To systematically characterize the intrinsic electronic structure and many-body photoemission effects in metallic platinum, resolving previously unidentified satellite features and providing a consistent spectroscopic reference for interpreting Pt-containing materials.
AI.method: Combined experimental approach using RHEELS, SXPS, and HAXPES, supported by ab initio DFT and G0W0 calculations with and without spin-orbit coupling.
AI.result: Identification of interband transitions, surface/bulk plasmons, plasmonic overtones, semi-core ionization losses, previously unresolved satellite features and spin-orbit splittings, and demonstration that relativistic effects are critical for reproducing Pt valence electronic structure.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a unified, internally consistent spectroscopic reference for metallic platinum, providing a robust framework for interpreting photoelectron spectra of Pt-containing catalysts, electronic materials, and related 5d transition metal systems.

title: Complete Raman Tensor Determination in Birefringent $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ by Single-Stage Hyperspectral Analysis of Polarization Angle-Resolved Raman Spectra
summary: The low symmetry of the monoclinic phase of Ga$_2$O$_3$ leads to pronounced optical anisotropy and, consequently, to birefringence, which strongly affects the Raman response. Because Raman scattering is fundamentally sensitive to the polarizability of a material, this anisotropy must be carefully accounted for in order to extract quantitative information - an effort that has only recently been shown to be feasible in such media. Here, we report Raman measurements from all three principal crystal planes $(100)$, $(010)$, and $(001)$, as well as from the $(\overline{2}01)$-plane of a $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ single crystal. By combining polarization angle-resolved Raman spectroscopy (PARRS) with a newly developed fitting procedure and explicitly accounting for birefringence, we achieve full spectral separation and quantitatively determine the energies and relative Raman tensor elements of all 15 Raman-active modes.

AI.tldr: This paper uses polarization angle-resolved Raman spectroscopy with a new fitting procedure that accounts for birefringence to fully separate and quantify the energies and relative Raman tensor elements of all 15 Raman-active modes in β-Ga₂O₃.
AI.motivation: The low symmetry of monoclinic β-Ga₂O₃ causes strong optical anisotropy and birefringence that complicates quantitative Raman analysis; accounting for this anisotropy has only recently become feasible.
AI.method: Raman measurements from three principal crystal planes (100), (010), (001) and the (͞201)-plane combined with polarization angle-resolved Raman spectroscopy (PARRS) and a newly developed fitting procedure that explicitly accounts for birefringence.
AI.result: Full spectral separation and quantitative determination of energies and relative Raman tensor elements for all 15 Raman-active modes of β-Ga₂O₃.
AI.conclusion: The birefringence-aware PARRS approach enables quantitative extraction of Raman parameters in strongly anisotropic monoclinic materials like β-Ga₂O₃.

title: Symmetry and Quantum Geometry in Bloch Bands
summary: Quantum geometric quantities have featured heavily in the discussion of the properties of quantum systems in recent years. Among quantities most commonly discussed is the variance of Berry curvature and the integral of the trace of the quantum metric tensor. Despite their usefulness, it is known that they suffer from one significant complication: for a tight-binding model, the quantum geometric quantities depend not only on the parameters of the tight-binding model itself, but also the real space geometry of the tight-binding model, the so-called "orbital embedding". One explicitly geometry-independent quantity is therefore the minimal value of the quantum geometric quantity out of all possible real space geometries. In this work, we demonstrate that, if the tight-binding model is compatible with certain spatial symmetries, then the real space geometry that minimizes the variance of the Berry curvature or the integral of the trace of the quantum metric tensor must obey all those spatial symmetries. We further show that the statement is applicable to systems with magnetic translation symmetries and other composite symmetries, with implications for the quantum geometry of the Hofstadter model.

AI.tldr: Quantum geometric quantities in tight-binding models depend on orbital embedding (real-space geometry). This work shows that if the model has spatial symmetries, the real-space geometry minimizing Berry curvature variance or quantum metric trace must obey those symmetries, extending to magnetic translation and composite symmetries like the Hofstadter model.
AI.motivation: Quantum geometric quantities (Berry curvature variance, quantum metric trace) are useful but depend on the arbitrary real-space geometry (orbital embedding) of tight-binding models, not just model parameters. A geometry-independent characterization requires finding minimal values over all possible real-space geometries, but the space of possibilities is large and structured.
AI.method: The authors prove that when a tight-binding model is compatible with spatial symmetries (including magnetic translation and composite symmetries), the real-space geometry that minimizes the Berry curvature variance or the trace of the quantum metric tensor must itself respect those symmetries. The proof is based on symmetry arguments constraining the optimization landscape.
AI.result: The minimizing real-space geometry inherits all spatial symmetries of the tight-binding model. This applies to magnetic translation symmetries and composite symmetries, with explicit implications for the quantum geometry of the Hofstadter model.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry constraints drastically simplify the search for geometry-independent quantum geometric quantities by restricting the optimization to symmetry-respecting geometries.

title: Tunnel magnetoresistance effect with a Cr-doped $\mathrm{RuO_{2}}(110)$ altermagnet
summary: Antiferromagnets can have a finite spin-polarization in the momentum space when their magnetic structure breaks the macroscopic time-reversal symmetry. This spin-polarization can produce a spin-polarized electric current even in antiferromagnets with vanishingly small net magnetizaton, which supports the antiferromagentic tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) effect. In this paper, using first-principles calculations, we study the TMR effect with a doped altermagnet $\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_{x}\mathrm{O}_{2}$ with $(110)$ orientation, whose collinear antiferromagnetic structure breaks the time-reversal symmetry macroscopically. The momentum-dependent spin-polarization combined with the $(110)$ crystal orientation makes the electric current spin-polarized through bulk $\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_{x}\mathrm{O}_{2}(110)$. We further calculate the TMR effect in the $\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_{x}\mathrm{O}_{2}(110)/\mathrm{TiO_{2}}(110)/\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_{x}\mathrm{O}_{2}(110)$ tunnel junction and show that a finite TMR effect emerges. Based on the analysis of the tunneling transport, the TMR effect is attributed to the spin polarized tunneling transport with momentum dependence and the interfacial magnetic structures, as well as the spin-polarized electric current in a bulk form of $\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_{x}\mathrm{O}_{2}(110)$.

AI.tldr: The paper uses first-principles calculations to study the tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) effect in altermagnet Ru₁₋ₓCrₓO₂(110) tunnel junctions, showing that momentum-dependent spin-polarization in this time-reversal-symmetry-breaking antiferromagnet enables finite TMR despite negligible net magnetization.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that antiferromagnets with broken macroscopic time-reversal symmetry can support a spin-polarized current and produce a finite tunnel magnetoresistance effect, expanding the potential of antiferromagnetic spintronics.
AI.method: First-principles calculations of spin-polarized transport in doped altermagnet Ru₁₋ₓCrₓO₂ with (110) orientation, combined with analysis of Ru₁₋ₓCrₓO₂(110)/TiO₂(110)/Ru₁₋ₓCrₓO₂(110) tunnel junctions.
AI.result: A finite TMR effect emerges in the tunnel junction, originating from momentum-dependent spin-polarized tunneling transport, interfacial magnetic structures, and the bulk spin-polarized current in Ru₁₋ₓCrₓO₂(110).
AI.conclusion: Altermagnets with broken time-reversal symmetry can produce a measurable TMR effect even with vanishingly small net magnetization, offering new pathways for antiferromagnetic spintronic devices.

title: Magneto-Caloric effect and Multiple magnetic phases in Al doped Ni2MnSn0.75Al0.25 Heusler Alloys
summary: Among Heusler compounds,Ni based alloys have been extensively investigated because they exhibit desirable properties such as high Curie temperatures, which are advantageous for advanced magnetic and spintronic devices.The effect of Al substitution on the magnetic ground state of Ni2MnSn was investigated using the Ni2MnSn0.75Al0.25 Heusler alloy.Temperature-dependent magnetisation measurements identify a second-order paramagnetic to ferromagnetic transition at TC is 734K,followed by a first-order martensitic transformation near 263K,demonstrating strong magnetostructural coupling.Curie Weiss analysis yields a positive Weiss temperature theta CW is 746.4K and an effective magnetic moment of 6.82muB,confirming the predominance of ferromagnetic exchange interactions. The bifurcation between the ZFC and FCW magnetization curves,together with non saturating hysteretic M vs H loops, indicates the coexistence of competing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions.Further magnetic investigations establish the formation of an interacting reentrant cluster glass state accompanied by an exchange-bias effect.The observed magnetic behavior is attributed to the modification of Mn Mn exchange interactions induced by Al substitution and the associated atomic disorder,resulting in a complex magnetic ground state.

AI.tldr: Al substitution in Ni2MnSn Heusler alloy (Ni2MnSn0.75Al0.25) induces a complex magnetic ground state with FM, AFM, reentrant cluster glass and exchange-bias effects, driven by modified Mn-Mn exchange interactions and atomic disorder.
AI.motivation: To understand how Al substitution affects the magnetic ground state of Ni2MnSn Heusler alloys, which are promising for high-temperature magnetic and spintronic applications.
AI.method: Temperature-dependent magnetization measurements, Curie-Weiss analysis, ZFC/FCW protocols, and M vs H hysteresis loop measurements on Ni2MnSn0.75Al0.25 alloy.
AI.result: Second-order PM→FM transition at TC=734K; first-order martensitic transformation at ~263K with strong magnetostructural coupling; positive θCW=746.4K and μeff=6.82μB; bifurcation of ZFC/FCW and non-saturating hysteresis indicate competing FM and AFM interactions; formation of interacting reentrant cluster glass with exchange-bias effect.
AI.conclusion: Al substitution modifies Mn-Mn exchange interactions and introduces atomic disorder, leading to a complex magnetic ground state comprising ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, cluster glass, and exchange-bias phenomena.
